content:
A note on project details This project took part during my internship at STMicroelectronics and I’m so grateful they gave me the opportunity to learn and explore mixed signal IC design and specifically pixel readout architectures. Some of the work I did is under a non disclosure agreement which prevents me from going into the details of the design, but I still want to share my experience and motivation for this project.
Why shutter type matters When I came in I did not know anything about pixel and I had to learn from scratch. Enthiusastic and motivated I worked during 3 months with my supervisor on a chip that incorporates a new pixel readout architecture, that had never been tested on silicon before. The main principle is simple, combine the advantages of rolling and global shutter and avoid their drawbacks.
When a camera sensor turns light into an image, it does not always capture every part of a moving scene at exactly the same time. With a rolling shutter, the sensor captures or reads the image one row at a time. When something moves quickly, different rows can represent different moments. The spinning fan below shows how that timing can distort the shape of moving objects.
A global shutter captures the scene across the sensor at the same time. This can represent fast motion more naturally. Achieving that can require extra pixel circuitry and storage, which brings its own design trade-offs.
It is exactly in this context that my project took place. Exploring a way to combine the advantages of both pixels, while keeping the architecture simple.
Type of Pixels The two pixels have some of the same parts, but they store and read the image in different ways. The 4T pixel is simpler. The global-shutter pixel adds storage capacitors so the image can be captured across the sensor at the same time and read later.
4T pixel The name 4T means the pixel has four transistors:
TX (transfer gate): Opens the path from the photodiode to the floating diffusion (FD). RESET: Clears the FD before a new measurement. Source follower: Buffers the FD voltage so it can be read without disturbing the FD. SELECT: Connects the pixel signal to the column so it can be read. During exposure, the photodiode collects charge from light. When TX turns on, that charge moves to the FD and changes its voltage. The source follower buffers this voltage, and SELECT connects it to the column. In this example, the sensor reads the rows one at a time, so it is a rolling-shutter pixel.
Global-shutter pixel The global-shutter pixel has the same photodiode, TX, FD, and RESET, but it also has extra transistors and capacitors:
TX: Moves charge from the photodiode to the FD when the pixel is captured. RST (reset): Resets the FD before the next capture. SF1: Buffers the FD voltage so it can be sampled. PC: Turns on the path that lets SF1 drive the sampling circuit. S1 and S2: Switch the signal onto capacitors C1 and C2. SF2: Buffers the stored voltage for readout. RS: Connects the pixel output to the column. The photodiode stores the light signal as charge (the charge domain). At the end of exposure, all pixels transfer their charge to the FD at the same time, where it becomes a voltage. S1 and S2 save voltage samples on C1 and C2. This is voltage-domain storage: the capacitors hold voltage, not the original photodiode charge. The camera can then read the stored voltages row by row, after the whole image has been captured.

content:
Project Overview The goal of this project is to design and layout a ripple carry adder for two 8 bit signed values. Addition and subtraction are supported, and overflow is detected. It is part of a bigger project, where I want to design an entire CPU core. For this reason, the bit pitch (size needed for one bit) is crucial as it will be used on other components such as the shifter.
For this specific design the critical path is determined by the carry propagation and it is essential to minimize it, by sizing the transistors correctly. The sizes are shown on the schematics and layouts below.
Circuit Design The overall design is made of 8 full adder stages, each of which output a sum and a carry. It supports two inputs, A and B, as well as a substract bit to choose from addition or substraction. I used xor gates to implement the substraction as it it basically take the 2’s complement of the B input and add it to A (with +1 from the first carry in). The overflow is detected by xor’ing the carry in and carry out of the most significant bit.
The overall design is shown below !
Let’s first build the XOR gate. We set the bit pitch to 2.91um for ease of routing and avoid DRC violations. It will also be easier for the full adder as it more complex and need more space for routing.
I then built a full adder from transistor-level logic. It is a pretty standard way of doing a full adder. Transistors are sized standardly using a minimum transistor width of 150 nm. Big PMOS transistors were also fingered to make them more compact and reduce the capacitance. Diffusion sharing was used as much as possible to reduce the area.
The physical layout of one full-adder stage is shown below.
Finally, putting everything together I got the following layout. We can clearly see the bit pitch matching for the xor and full adder which facilitates the routing. As a side note, I strictly used M1 and M2 metals for the xor and full adder layout and kept M3 for the overall routing.
Verification and Critical Path Timing I then verified the design with a pulse voltage source and text-file test vectors. For the signed 8-bit range of -128 to 127, I used -1 + 1 = 0 as an example and traced both the input and output signals in simulation.
Input A is initially 11111111, the 8-bit two’s-complement representation of -1. At 5 ns its sign bit changes, making A equal to 127.
B changes from 0 to 1 at 4 ns while subtraction remains disabled, setting up the -1 + 1 test.
The output trace shows the sum bits responding in sequence as the carry propagates from the least significant bit toward the most significant bit. I measured delay from the 50% voltage crossings: B0 at 4.01 ns and Sum7 at 4.38 ns. This gives a critical-path delay of 370 ps.
The sum settles to 00000000. Sum7 is the last sum bit to cross the 50% threshold after the input transition, giving a 370 ps critical path delay. When A changes to 127 at 5 ns while B stays at 1, overflow asserts because the result is out of range.
Conclusion & Final Notes And this is the end of this post ! There are definitely ways of improving this design but the main goal was to have a working adder. The learning curve of learning virtuoso is steep but this kind of project is really helpful. Hope this post helps if you are designing your own adder !

content:
A tiny processor, one step at a time A processor can seem like a mysterious box that turns instructions into results. For a small project, we can just consider some parts of it, and break it into a few simple pieces.
I wrote a small processor in Verilog. It has four 8 bit registers, a shared 8 bit bus, and arithmetic logic for adding or subtracting. Inside the code, the processor is more like a little control room where each piece does its work one step at a time.
The control room: an FSM The processor uses a finite state machine (FSM) to decide what to do next. It is a little bit like a manager following a checklist: wait for a job, collect the instruction, understand it, do the work, and signal that the step is complete.
Here are the states from my code:
parameter [2:0] S_IDLE = 3'b000, S_FETCH = 3'b001, S_DECODE = 3'b010, S_EXEC = 3'b011, S_WRITE = 3'b100; In simple words, here is what each state does:
Idle: wait for the w signal to say an instruction is ready. Fetch: save the instruction fields (F, Rx, and Ry). Decode: identify which operation and registers were selected. Execute: choose control signals and perform the operation. Write: raise Done to show that this pass is finished, then return to idle. The drawing below is a map I drew representing that sequence and the operation paths.
The kitchen analogy The four registers (R0 through R3) are like labeled storage bins. The shared bus is the countertop: only one bin should put its value on the countertop at a time, and another part can take that value from there.
The ALU is the calculator on the countertop (a little bit like kitchen utensils manipulating ingredients). For addition and subtraction, it uses the value saved in A and the value currently on the bus:
OP_ADD: G <= A + BusWires; OP_SUB: G <= A - BusWires; G holds the answer until the write state puts it back into the destination register.
The instructions The two-bit F field selects one of four simple instructions:
00: load the input Data into Rx. 01: move the value in Ry into Rx. 10: add Rx and Ry, saving the answer in Rx. 11: subtract Ry from Rx, saving the answer in Rx. The complete processor is below. The FSM is the checklist, and the registers, bus, and ALU are the workshop tools it coordinates.
Complete Verilog code `timescale 1ns / 1ps module proc (Data, Resetn, w, Clock, F, Rx, Ry, Done, BusWires); input [7:0] Data; input Resetn, w, Clock; input [1:0] F, Rx, Ry; output wire Done; output reg [7:0] BusWires; localparam [2:0] S_IDLE = 3'b000, S_FETCH = 3'b001, S_DECODE = 3'b010, S_EXEC = 3'b011, S_WRITE = 3'b100; localparam [1:0] OP_LOAD = 2'b00, OP_MOVE = 2'b01, OP_ADD = 2'b10, OP_SUB = 2'b11; reg [2:0] state; reg [1:0] opcode, destination, source; reg [7:0] immediate, A, G; reg [7:0] registers [0:3]; integer i; assign Done = (state == S_WRITE); always @(*) begin BusWires = 8'b0; case (state) S_EXEC: begin if (opcode == OP_LOAD) BusWires = immediate; else BusWires = registers[source]; end S_WRITE: BusWires = G; default: BusWires = 8'b0; endcase end always @(posedge Clock or negedge Resetn) begin if (!Resetn) begin state <= S_IDLE; opcode <= OP_LOAD; destination <= 2'b00; source <= 2'b00; immediate <= 8'b0; A <= 8'b0; G <= 8'b0; for (i = 0; i < 4; i = i + 1) registers[i] <= 8'b0; end else begin case (state) S_IDLE: begin if (w) state <= S_FETCH; end S_FETCH: begin opcode <= F; destination <= Rx; source <= Ry; immediate <= Data; state <= S_DECODE; end S_DECODE: begin if ((opcode == OP_ADD) || (opcode == OP_SUB)) A <= registers[destination]; state <= S_EXEC; end S_EXEC: begin case (opcode) OP_LOAD: G <= BusWires; OP_MOVE: G <= BusWires; OP_ADD: G <= A + BusWires; OP_SUB: G <= A - BusWires; default: G <= 8'b0; endcase state <= S_WRITE; end S_WRITE: begin registers[destination] <= BusWires; state <= S_IDLE; end default: state <= S_IDLE; endcase end end endmodule

Project Overview I designed a transistor-level 1.2 V bandgap voltage reference that generates a stable voltage across temperature and process variations. In general, it is super important for a circuit to have a stable reference voltage otherwise some components might behave in the wrong way. When I say stable, I mean that the voltage should not change, or change very minimally, with temperature and process variations. So I designed a bandgap reference that uses the opposing temperature dependencies of two voltage components to produce a stable output.
What I Designed Built a temperature-compensated reference using PTAT and CTAT voltage components. Designed the bipolar devices, current mirrors, and feedback circuitry in Cadence Virtuoso. Combined the opposing temperature dependencies to produce a stable 1.2 V output. Characterization I evaluated the reference with Cadence Spectre across the conditions that matter for an integrated analog circuit:
Temperature sweeps Power supply rejection ratio (PSRR) Noise and power consumption Process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corners Monte Carlo mismatch analysis Physical Verification I verified the physical IC layout was DRC and LVS clean. Parasitic extraction was also performed to compare pre-layout and post-layout performance to understand the impact of physical implementation on the circuit.

content:
Project Goal I designed a digital piano on an FPGA that turns switch and push-button inputs into musical notes. The system decodes the selected note, generates the correct tone using a clock divider, and displays the note and octave on a four-digit seven-segment display.
How It Works Encoded the seven natural notes using one-hot switch inputs. Used push-buttons to select flats, sharps, and the upper octave. Converted the selected note into a divider value based on the desired audio frequency. Generated the speaker clock with a counter and toggle-based clock divider. Scanned the seven-segment display to show the note letter, octave, and sharp indicator. Added reset and silence behavior for invalid or empty switch combinations. Verification I created VHDL testbench stimulus to exercise the complete range of inputs, including all seven notes, sharps, flats, octave changes, silence, rapid switching, and non-sequential note changes. The simulations confirmed that the input signals and display outputs responded to the programmed test cases.
The design also revealed a practical limitation of behavioral simulation: the FPGA’s MMCM clock manager requires hardware timing to lock, so some downstream outputs remain uninitialized in simulation even while the input stimulus is applied correctly.
Project Graphs & Figures These figures document the main verification steps from the lab report.
The CLK, counter, trigger, CLK_OUT, and ONE_SHOT signals show how the input clock becomes the audio clock.
The target-versus-actual note-frequency graph verifies the divider calculations used for the piano notes.
The Vivado waveform shows switch_in cycling through C to B, modifier changes, reset behavior, and rapid note switching.
Conclusion & Final Notes It is a pretty fun and hands on project I would recommend to anobody interested in learning FPGA and hardware description languages. What I like the most about this project is the final physical result, just being able to play and hear the notes is super satisfying.

In Summary This project builds a visual localization pipeline that estimates a drone’s GPS position by matching its camera feed against a pre-loaded satellite map — no GPS, no wireless signal required. It compares two classical feature matching algorithms, SIFT and ORB, and tests them under various degraded image conditions to find out where each one breaks down.
Context & Motivation I have always been fascinated by the idea that a machine can look at the world and figure out where it is, the same way you might recognize a neighborhood from a window seat on a plane. When I came across the problem of GPS-denied drone navigation, it felt like the perfect intersection of computer vision, real-world constraints, and genuinely high stakes applications — search and rescue, military operations, remote exploration. The question that really hooked me was not just “can we do this?” but “how robust is it really?” Most research papers test their algorithms under near-perfect conditions, but in the real world, images are blurry, noisy, and low resolution. I wanted to know exactly at what point the system stops working — and whether the choice of algorithm actually matters. What I Did Built a full localization pipeline in Python using OpenCV and rasterio, matching drone images against a satellite map through feature detection, descriptor matching, and homography estimation Implemented and compared two feature detectors: SIFT, known for its accuracy and scale robustness, and ORB, a faster binary alternative Used the UAV-VisLoc dataset, a large-scale benchmark containing 6,742 drone images paired with satellite maps across 11 locations in China — focusing on a single location covering roughly 64 km² in the Taizhou region Divided the satellite map into overlapping tiles and matched each drone image against every tile independently, selecting the best match by inlier count Ran five independent degradation experiments motion blur, Gaussian noise, and resolution reduction on drone images, and resolution reduction on the satellite map to identify failure thresholds for each algorithm Results The results were honest and a little humbling. SIFT was the only algorithm that worked at all — ORB failed entirely across every single condition, including the clean baseline, because the scale difference between drone and satellite imagery simply exceeded what its scale pyramid could handle. That was not what I expected going in. SIFT held up surprisingly well under Gaussian noise, maintaining a 100% success rate at both noise levels tested. Motion blur was the most damaging degradation, with success rate dropping to 40% at a blur kernel of 5 pixels and collapsing to 20% at kernel 15. Resolution reduction told a similar story — robust at moderate levels, then a sharp cliff at higher factors. The localization errors were large in absolute terms (around 4000–5000 meters on an 8.86 km map), which means the pipeline is finding something but not with useful precision. In this context, success rate turned out to be a far more informative metric than raw localization error.
Conclusion & Final Notes This project taught me that negative results are results too. I went in expecting a clean speed–accuracy tradeoff between SIFT and ORB, and instead found that ORB was simply not geometrically capable of handling this task — a much more interesting finding in its own way. If I were to do this again, I would test on a much larger image sample (the full 768 images rather than just 5), explore preprocessing steps like contrast enhancement to help with cross-view matching, and investigate whether tuning ORB’s scale pyramid parameters could make it viable. The pipeline works, but there is a lot of room to make it work better — and now I know exactly where to look.

I Built a Robot That Understands Sign Language The Idea I wanted to build a robot that you could control just by showing it hand signs, no remote, no keyboard, just American Sign Language (ASL). The goal was to keep it simple, fast, and cheap enough for anyone to build.
How It Works The system has two main parts:
A camera mounted on a small robot (built with a Raspberry Pi) A nearby laptop that does the “thinking” The robot takes a picture of your hand sign and sends it wirelessly to the laptop. The laptop figures out which sign you made and sends the answer back. The robot then moves in that direction.
I used four signs, each one is both a letter and a direction:
L = Left R = Right N = North (forward) S = South (backward) Teaching the Robot to “See” To recognize signs, I needed a lot of hand pictures to train a model. I used three sets of images:
A big public dataset from Kaggle (mostly plain backgrounds) My own photos, taken with messier, more realistic backgrounds A mix of both Training on more varied images helped the robot recognize signs in real rooms, not just in perfect lighting.
The Brain Behind It Instead of building a neural network from scratch, I used two existing, well-tested models (VGG16 and DenseNet201) and combined them together. Each one is good at spotting different kinds of details in an image. By merging their strengths, the combined model was much better at recognizing signs it hadn’t seen in that exact setting before, kind of like getting a second opinion before making a decision.
The architecture of the combined model looks like this: Does It Actually Work? Yes, pretty well:
On test data, the combined model reached up to 97% accuracy. In live, real-world testing (different people, different backgrounds), it got things right about 70% of the time. Each prediction took about 0.24 seconds, and the whole process (camera to robot movement) took under 3 seconds, fast enough to feel responsive. I also tested it with people of different skin tones. It worked a bit less reliably there, which shows the training data needs to be more diverse going forward.
What’s Next This was a first step. Future versions could:
Recognize more signs, including moving (dynamic) ones Work better across different skin tones and lighting Let the robot do more than just move, like picking up objects or navigating on its own Why It Matters Projects like this show that sign-language-controlled devices don’t need expensive, complicated hardware to work. With just a Raspberry Pi and a regular laptop, it’s possible to build something useful for accessibility and hands-free control, and to do it in a way that’s fast enough for real use.

content:
Introduction Analog communication systems were the first and dominant form of communication used in modern history. From transmitting your voice through a telephone line to listening to radio and watching television, analog communication is hidden everywhere !
But why analog communication and what does “analog” mean in this context ? You might be disappointed by how short the answer is, but put simply, analog means continuous. In other words an analog signal is a function that can take up any value within a continuous range.
One way to think about how analog communication appeared is that most natural phenomena are in fact continuous and hence an intuitive way to capture their entirety is by using a continuous system. Of course, technology was also the main limiting factor. When Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone in 1876 (long before the famous Bell Labs was formally established in 1925), none of the technology required to digitize a continuous signal existed, so digital wasn’t even an option!
Going back to analog signals and communication, let’s take temperature as an example, although one might round its value to an integer, it is a continuous value. Height, time or even voltage are other examples. And surprisingly enough, when you want to capture your voice to send it to your neighbor (with a telephone !), a natural way to proceed is by representing it as a continuous signal. Think about it for a second, as you speak the air pressure changes smoothly taking up any value over time - it is the exact definition of a continuous function, or analog signal - perfect to transmit to our neighbor.
Generalizing this example, it is easy to convince yourself that analog is the right choice for cases where you want to transmit continuous information ! We will see, this might not be always true but for now let’s keep in mind this example and let’s dive deeper into the theory behind analog communication.
Analog Communication Theory There are three main types of modulation in analog communication Amplitude Modulation (AM), Frequency Modulation (FM) and Phase Modulation (PM). You might be wondering now what modulation mean, and it is a fair question to ask, in simple terms it means applying your original signal to a another high frequency signal called a carrier wave. It might seem abastract, but it will make more sense in the following paragarphs. For now though, I will say that increasing the frequency of the original signal is necessary for two reasons. To make it travel further (low frequency signals loose energy quickly !) and use smaller antennas to receive the signal (an antenna of length 1/4 of the wavelength transmitted is required !).
AM AM was developed in the first quarter of the 20th century and was mostly used for radio broadcasting. It is straightforward and consist of three main parts
$$ s(t) = A_c \bigl[1 + \mu m(t)\bigr] \cos\left(2\pi f_c t\right) $$
Let’s break it down. $A_c$ is the amplitude of the carrier wave, simply how strong the carrier is to begin with. $m(t)$ is nothing more than your original message (your voice for example !), and $\mu$, called the modulation index, controls how much the message is allowed to affect the amplitude of the carrier. Finally $\cos(2\pi f_c t)$ is the carrier wave itself, oscillating at frequency $f_c$. Put together, what AM does is make the amplitude of the carrier follow the shape of your message - the louder you speak, the bigger the swing in amplitude !
This simplicity is exactly why AM was so popular for radio broadcasting, the receiver only needs to detect how the amplitude changes over time to recover the original message, which is a fairly cheap operation. But this simplicity comes at a cost, since most of the noise picked up along the way (lightning, electrical interference, you name it !) also affects amplitude, AM signals tend to be quite noisy, you have probably experienced this yourself if you ever listened to AM radio !
FM FM was developed later, in the 1930s, by Edwin Armstrong, mainly to solve the noise problem we just talked about. Instead of varying the amplitude of the carrier, FM varies its frequency, while keeping the amplitude constant.
$$ s(t) = A_c \cos\left(2\pi f_c t + 2\pi k_f \int_0^t m(\tau) d\tau\right) $$
Here again $A_c$ and $f_c$ play the same role as before, the amplitude and frequency of the carrier. $k_f$ is the frequency sensitivity, it tells you how much the frequency should shift for a given value of the message $m(t)$. The integral might look intimidating but all it really says is that the instantaneous frequency of the carrier is constantly adjusted by the value of the message at each point in time.
Because the information is now carried by the frequency and not the amplitude, FM signals are much less sensitive to the kind of noise that affects amplitude. This is the reason why FM radio (the 88-108 MHz band you are used to !) sounds so much clearer than AM, at the cost of needing a wider bandwidth to transmit the signal.
PM PM, for its part, takes a similar idea but instead varies the phase of the carrier rather than its frequency.
$$ s(t) = A_c \cos\left(2\pi f_c t + k_p m(t)\right) $$
$k_p$ here is the phase sensitivity, equivalent to $k_f$ for FM, and it controls how much the message shifts the phase of the carrier. You might notice that FM and PM look very alike, and they are, in fact PM and FM are mathematically related to each other (one is essentially the derivative of the other !), which is why they are often grouped together. FM was historically more popular for analog broadcasting, but PM ended up being more useful for digital communication, where it became the basis for modulation schemes still used today like PSK (Phase Shift Keying).
Conclusion So there you have it, three different ways of carrying a message over a carrier wave, by playing with its amplitude, frequency or phase. AM, simple but noisy, FM, clearer but requiring more bandwidth, and PM, less common on its own but foundational to a lot of what came after.
Going back to our original question, why analog communication, I hope it is now clearer how naturally continuous signals like your voice fit into this framework, and why for most of the 20th century, this was simply the only way to communicate over long distances. Of course, as we will see in a future post, digital communication eventually took over for most applications, but it is worth remembering that the theory behind it owes a lot to the analog systems we just covered !

Hi, I’m Vassily, a rising senior at Columbia University studying Computer Engineering.
This past summer I worked at STMicroelectronics on pixel design and characterization for optical sensors. I previously worked at a startup in Paris on LLMs architecture design and also in a biomedical lab at Columbia University on a project involving ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM).
My research interests range from VLSI low-power design to sensor and mixed-signal circuit design. I have always loved playing with robots, sensors, and all kinds of connected objects, but what fascinates me is the chips inside! content: Descartes’ Meditations on First Philosophy is not an easy read, I will warn you from the start ! This one requires patience and a bit of philosophical backbone. Descartes takes you on a journey of radical doubt, systematically questioning everything he thinks he knows until he reaches what he considers to be the only unquestionable truth : the famous “cogito, ergo sum” (I think, therefore I am !). From there, he rebuilds his entire understanding of reality, tackling everything from the nature of mind and body to the existence of God. Fair warning though, this is not the book to read casually on the beach and you will find yourself reading the same sentences over and over again to understand them…

content: Sartre’s Nausea follows Antoine Roquentin, a melancholic and socially isolated intellectual living in Bouville while he works on a biography of a historical figure. He finds himself affeceted by a persistent nausea which, while he struggles to understand it at first, we might nowadays simply call depression. The book is powerful and surprisingly easy to read, and I recommend it for anyone interested in questioning their own feelings and views of the world !

content: Mary Beard’s SPQR meticulously describes the history of Rome, sharing details that go far beyond the usual tales of emperors and military conquests. Beard takes you through the city’s rise from a small settlement to a vast empire, but what makes it special is how she focuses on the everyday lives of ordinary Romans (the slaves, merchants, and citizens you rarely hear about !). If you have ever wondered what Rome was actually like beyond the textbook, this is the book for you !

content: The Red and the Black by Stendhal is such a fascinating read. Beyond the crazy storyline, the intense characters, and all the psychological drama, I really like being immersed in the 19th century. It makes me think of how france, where I grew up, was a few centuries ago and I can definitely see its influence on how modern French society has evolved. Also, the story happens right after the Napoleonic wars, and the author makes subtle references to them, which feels like a nice easter egg when reading. In short, definitely read this book, but make sure to have enough time because it is a long book!
